draft.title: Gel electrophoresis
card: DNA fragments are loaded into wells at one end of a gel. An electric field is then applied across the gel.
DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so the fragments move toward the positive electrode.
The gel slows large fragments more than small ones. Small fragments travel further, so the fragments end up sorted by size.
The fragments show as bands. Comparing the band patterns of different samples is used in DNA profiling, such as matching crime scene DNA to a suspect.
draft.remember: Negative DNA runs to the positive end. Smaller fragments go further.

a.q: After electrophoresis, which DNA fragment will be closest to the positive electrode?
opts: The fragment that was loaded first
The fragment with the most bands
a.why: The gel slows large fragments more, so the smallest fragment travels furthest toward the positive electrode. The order of loading does not decide how far a fragment moves.
a.clue: Which fragments move through the gel most easily?

b.q: A detective compares DNA bands from a crime scene with bands from two suspects. How can the gel show that one suspect's DNA matches?
opts: That suspect's bands line up with the scene's bands
That suspect's bands sit nearest the wells
That suspect has more bands than the scene sample
That suspect's bands are darker than the others
b.why: Matching fragment sizes travel the same distance, so the bands line up. Position in the gel shows size, so being near the wells or having more bands does not show a match.
b.clue: Same size fragments travel the same distance.

b.best: That suspect's bands line up with the scene's bands
